source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974) Judgment under uncertainty: heuristics and biases. Science 185:1124-1131
finding: Founding statement. Three heuristics (representativeness, availability, anchoring and adjustment) are economical and usually work, but cause systematic, predictable errors. Representativeness: probability is judged by similarity to a stereotype (Steve the shy librarian).
numbers: Subjects ordered occupations by probability and by similarity 'in exactly the same way'. The paper lists biases: insensitivity to prior probability, to sample size, to predictability, misconceptions of chance and regression, retrievability, imaginability, illusory correlation, insufficient adjustment, conjunctive and disjunctive events, overconfident intervals.
quote: Biases in judgments reveal some heuristics of thinking under uncertainty.
limits: A list of biases, not a process model. The heuristics are named after the fact. Many numbers are from earlier, cited studies, not run in this paper.
agent_relevance: S1 can treat 'a vivid description' and 'a number in the prompt' as two known cue types that capture judgment. Both bias sources are things code can detect and move out of the task text.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974) Judgment under uncertainty: heuristics and biases. Science 185:1124-1131 (base-rate paradigm)
finding: Base-rate neglect: subjects judged whether a described person was an engineer or lawyer. The stated base rate (70 engineers/30 lawyers vs 30/70) was ignored when a description was present, even a worthless one. With no description, priors were used correctly.
numbers: Bayes odds ratio between the two conditions should be (.7/.3)^2 = 5.44; subjects gave 'essentially the same' probabilities in both. For the worthless description of Dick, the judged probability was .5 in both base-rate conditions. With no description, they used .7 and .3.
quote: When no specific evidence is given, prior probabilities are properly utilized; when worthless evidence is given, prior probabilities are ignored
limits: Described as a summary of Kahneman and Tversky 1973. The Science paper gives no N. Later work (Bar-Hillel 1980; Koehler 1996) shows base-rate use varies with causal relevance and format.
agent_relevance: Key point for the agent: worthless extra text can switch off a correct prior. Irrelevant detail in a prompt is not neutral. It can replace a base rate the model would otherwise use.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974) Judgment under uncertainty: heuristics and biases. Science 185:1124-1131 (sample size and chance)
finding: Insensitivity to sample size (hospital problem): the larger hospital has about 45 births a day, the smaller about 15. Which one records more days with over 60 percent boys? Most subjects said the two are about equally likely, because both samples share the same statistic.
numbers: Answers: larger hospital 21, smaller hospital 21, about the same 53 (counts as printed in the paper; the paper gives no N for this item in the text). Correct answer: smaller hospital.
limits: The sampling-theory logic is clean but the item is a single vignette; later 'sample size' work found sensitivity rises when the size cue is made salient (not opened this session).
agent_relevance: A cheap, code-checkable test item for S0/S4: the model should be asked once and checked against the known answer.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974) Judgment under uncertainty: heuristics and biases. Science 185:1124-1131 (anchoring paradigm)
finding: Anchoring and insufficient adjustment. A number from a spun wheel of fortune (0 to 100) was shown, subjects said higher or lower, then gave the estimate (the percentage of African countries in the UN). Estimates were pulled toward the arbitrary number. Payoffs for accuracy did not remove the effect.
numbers: Median estimate of the percentage of African UN members: 25 for the group given 10, and 45 for the group given 65. Factorial estimate in 5 seconds: ascending 1x2x...x8 median 512; descending 8x7x...x1 median 2,250; the true value is 40,320.
quote: Different groups were given different numbers for each quantity, and these arbitrary numbers had a marked effect on estimates.
limits: Original theory: the pull comes from adjustment that stops too soon. Later work (Strack and Mussweiler 1997; Epley and Gilovich 2001, 2006) offers selective-accessibility and mixed accounts. See a18 and a22.
agent_relevance: The wheel was random and obviously irrelevant, and it still moved estimates by 20 points. This is the human model of why S1 input hygiene needs a code step: a stated guess in the prompt acts as an anchor.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974) Judgment under uncertainty: heuristics and biases. Science 185:1124-1131 (availability and calibration)
finding: Availability: frequency is judged by ease of recall or construction. Words starting with K vs K as third letter; committees of 2 vs 8 members. Calibration: 98 percent confidence intervals were too narrow.
numbers: Committees from 10 people: median estimate for committees of 2 was 70 and for 8 was 20; the correct answer is 45 for both. Intervals meant to hold the truth 98 percent of the time (X01 to X99) missed it for about 30 percent of the problems. Illusory correlation (Chapman and Chapman) persisted even when the true correlation was negative.
limits: Availability is defined loosely (recall ease vs imagined ease). Later work separates content from experienced ease (Schwarz et al. 1991; not opened).
agent_relevance: Overconfident intervals match the agent-side finding that stated confidence overshoots hit rates (G-level guardrail on verbal confidence, section 4b).

source: Kahneman & Tversky (1972/1973) On the psychology of prediction (Oregon Research Institute bulletin 12(4), Oct 1972; Psych Review 1973)
finding: Tom W. study. Likelihood rankings of nine graduate fields tracked similarity to the stereotype almost perfectly and ignored base rates. People knew the base rates when asked, but did not use them.
numbers: Mean likelihood vs mean similarity r = .97; mean likelihood vs estimated base rate r = -.65. More than 95 percent judged Tom W. more likely to study computer science than humanities or education, although these have larger enrolment. A second group (N = 69) rated similarity. Median hit-rate estimate for predictions from projective tests: 23 percent (low trust in the description did not change the ranking).
quote: Judgments of likelihood essentially coincide with judgments of similarity
limits: Only 24 percent of respondents considered that the description might be inaccurate. A 1972 bulletin; the published 1973 version may differ in detail. Same design replicated in more samples in the bulletin.
agent_relevance: The ranking uses similarity even when the person knows the description is of poor validity. For the agent: telling it the source is unreliable (without code removing it) may not change the order of candidates.

source: Kahneman & Tversky (1972/1973) On the psychology of prediction (Oregon Research Institute bulletin 12(4), Oct 1972; Psych Review 1973) (engineer-lawyer and cab problem)
finding: Two direct tests of Bayes. (1) Engineer/lawyer: five descriptions, high-engineer (N = 86) vs low-engineer (N = 85) group. (2) Cab problem: 85 percent blue cabs, a witness correct 4 times in 5.
numbers: Engineer/lawyer: the mean probability was 50 percent for group L and 55 percent for group H (t = 3.23, df = 169, p < .01), where the correct shift is large; every point lay closer to the identity line than to the Bayes line. Null description: judged 70 and 30 percent. Cab: median 80 percent for the base-rate-only group (N = 36); with the witness the median was 20 percent (N = 35); Bayes gives about 41 percent, so the base rate was 'completely suppressed'.
limits: The cab problem is the source of later arguments about causal vs statistical base rates. Bar-Hillel and Koehler showed base rates are used when they look causal or relevant; not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Gives exact human reference numbers for a base-rate test on the agent: a model that says 20 percent shows the same pattern as the 1972 humans (the result in Binz and Schulz 2022 was the opposite for GPT-3, see a25).

source: Kahneman & Tversky (1972/1973) On the psychology of prediction (Oregon Research Institute bulletin 12(4), Oct 1972; Psych Review 1973) (regression)
finding: Numerical prediction is not regressive. Subjects predicting a student's grade percentile from a measure they were told was unreliable still gave extreme, input-matched predictions.
numbers: Three groups predicted GPA from percentile GPA (N = 32), a mental concentration test (N = 37) and sense of humor. No significant difference between predictions from percentile GPA and from mental concentration. Predictions from sense of humor were regressive, but not enough (implied correlation above .70).
quote: people fail to regress when predicting from an input however unreliable which is regarded as a measure of the outcome variable
limits: Group Ns for the third group not captured here. Regression neglect is one of the best-replicated findings of the program (not re-checked here against a failed replication).
agent_relevance: Relevant for any step where the agent predicts a numeric value from a noisy cue, such as a pass rate from a single sample.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1983) Extensional versus intuitive reasoning: the conjunction fallacy in probability judgment. Psych Review 90:293-315
finding: Linda problem and conjunction fallacy. Subjects judge that Linda is a feminist bank teller (T&F) more probable than a bank teller (T), which breaks the conjunction rule P(A&B) <= P(A). The probability ranking follows representativeness, not extension.
numbers: Representativeness ranking: 87 percent (Bill) and 85 percent (Linda) showed the predicted order (N = 88 UBC undergraduates). Direct tests: violations in 12 of 12 comparisons, overall 88 percent. Probability and representativeness mean ranks correlated .96 (Bill) and .98 (Linda). Statistical sophistication made no difference in Table 1 tests. In the transparent test, 85 percent ranked T&F above T.
quote: Perhaps the simplest and the most basic qualitative law of probability is the conjunction rule
limits: Between-subject (indirect) tests also showed the effect, so it is not only a within-subject artefact. Alternative readings (T read as 'T and not F') were tested and rejected in the paper: 57 percent still erred with the 'whether or not' wording (n = 75).
agent_relevance: A clean benchmark for 'does the agent follow extension': rank-by-fit instead of rank-by-probability is exactly what S3/S7 voters can do. Code can check P(A&B) <= P(A) on any pair of answers.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1983) Extensional versus intuitive reasoning: the conjunction fallacy in probability judgment. Psych Review 90:293-315 (attempts to remove the error)
finding: Telling people about the rule, giving a betting format, or asking graduate students helped only partly. A valid-vs-resemblance argument was still lost by most. Frequency wording reduced errors.
numbers: Choosing the invalid resemblance argument: 65 percent (n = 58). Betting task: 56 percent violations (n = 60). Social-science graduate students with statistics credit (N = 64): 36 percent erred, mean rating T&F 3.5 vs T 3.8. For the 'whether or not' version the 57 percent error rate stayed. Health-survey item: 65 percent errors with percentages (N = 147), 25 percent when the question was posed as 'how many of 100' (N = 117), 11 percent when estimating the base group first (N = 360).
limits: These are the strongest early boundary conditions: format and an explicit count help a lot. Later work (Hertwig and Gigerenzer 1999; Tentori et al. 2013) disputes how much of the error is a language effect; not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports a code-side fix rather than an instruction: ask for counts or nested sets before asking for probability. Instruction-only debiasing is the weak option (section 4b).

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1983) Extensional versus intuitive reasoning: the conjunction fallacy in probability judgment. Psych Review 90:293-315 (domain breadth)
finding: The conjunction error also appears with medical symptoms, sports forecasts, and causal scenarios. Experts were not immune. Adding a plausible cause raised the conjunction's estimate.
numbers: Medical diagnoses (Stanford and UBC, 5 problems): 91 percent average violations, range 73 to 100 percent. Borg tennis (N = 93): 72 percent ranked the conjunction above the constituent. Sub-4-minute-mile and sub-1:55 second half: 76 percent (N = 96). Earthquake and flood in California 1983: geometric means 3.1 percent vs 2.2 percent for flood alone (N = 245). The paper says it tested 'more than 3,000 subjects on dozens' of problems.
limits: All are 1980-82 student or conference samples. The paper reports that its problems were built to produce errors, so the rates are not a population estimate.
agent_relevance: A causal story makes a conjunction look likelier. An agent that writes a story first (S2/S3) may raise its own conjunctive claims; code should count the number of conditions in a claim.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1983) Citation Classic note on their 1974 Science paper (Current Contents 14)
finding: The authors' own history. The program began in 1969 and the 1974 paper summarised it. Their stated three-part method: compare intuition with normative rules, search for heuristics and the biases they bring, explore the gap between judgment and rational belief theory.
numbers: Cited over 420 times by April 1983 in the Social Sciences Citation Index. 'We spent the better part of 1973 writing the paper'.
limits: Self-report. The method is comparison with a normative rule, which is the very step Gigerenzer later attacks (a21).
agent_relevance: Useful framing for G-level design: the agent needs a normative rule that code can run (a count, a Bayes update), not an opinion about what is rational.

source: Gigerenzer & Hoffrage (1995) How to improve Bayesian reasoning without instruction: frequency formats. Psych Review 102:684-704
finding: The same Bayes problems are solved far more often when the numbers are given as natural frequencies (e.g. 10 in 1000 have the disease) than as probabilities. Natural frequencies make the Bayes calculation a simple ratio of counts.
numbers: Study 1: 60 Salzburg students, 15 problems. Bayesian algorithms in 16 percent of probability-format answers (standard menu) vs 46 percent in frequency format (standard menu); short menu 28 vs 50 percent. Format effect about 3 times the menu effect (about 29.9 and 21.6 vs 12.1 and 3.7 points). Study 2: 15 Konstanz students, 72 problems each.
quote: when information was presented in frequency formats, statistically naive participants derived up to 50% of all inferences by Bayesian algorithms
limits: Counts of correct final answers are lower than counts of Bayesian algorithms. 50 percent is a ceiling for naive participants, so half still fail. Practice alone gave 'virtually no increase' in the first 36 tasks.
agent_relevance: Direct design rule for S2/S4: convert probabilities in a task into counts of cases before asking the model to combine them. Code can do the conversion.

source: Chapman & Liu (2009) Numeracy, frequency, and Bayesian reasoning. Judgment and Decision Making 4:34-40
finding: Replicates the frequency-format gain, but shows it is carried mainly by high-numeracy people. Low-numerate people stayed near zero in both formats.
numbers: N = 346 students analysed (342 in the abstract). Median split on an 11-item numeracy scale: high n = 190, low n = 156. Correct answers (Down's syndrome item 47.62 percent, drunk-driving item 9.91 percent) were rare. Common wrong answers: 90 percent (the test hit rate) and 55 percent. Significant interaction of format by numeracy in a logistic regression.
limits: Online survey, only two items per person. Shows the gain is not general.
agent_relevance: Format conversion is a help only if the solver can then do the arithmetic. For an LLM the equivalent is a tool for the division; do not rely on the model to do it in its head.

source: Stock, Fisk & Montgomery (repository copy, year approximate) Measures of Bayesian reasoning performance on normal and natural frequency tasks
finding: Frequencies reduced over-estimation but did not reduce base-rate neglect errors. Older adults were unaffected by the format.
numbers: Study 1 compared probability and normalised frequency formats in older (60+) and younger (18-29) groups. Study 2 used natural frequencies. The abstract reports no association between format and avoidance of errors such as base-rate neglect.
limits: Preprint-style repository copy; sample sizes not extracted this session. A failed-extension case, not a failed replication of the 1995 headline.
agent_relevance: A reminder that the format fix is partial: it improves magnitude, not always the structure of the error.

source: Jonsson & Hampton (2006) The inverse conjunction fallacy. J Memory and Language 55:317-334
finding: Competing account: the conjunction effect is a case of intensional (similarity-based) reasoning. People accept 'all sofas have X' but reject or doubt 'all uncomfortable handmade sofas have X'. The more general statement gets more belief, which is the reverse of the conjunction rule.
numbers: Experiment 1: unmodified sentences got 21 percent more yes responses than modified ones; nearly three quarters of unmodified but only half of modified statements were endorsed as universally true. Experiment 2: some form of inverse conjunction fallacy on 56 percent of sentence pairs. Experiments 4 and 5 changed quantifiers ('every single', '100 percent') and used direct comparison: the effect barely moved. Experiment 4 mean confidence for yes: 8.3 vs 6.8 of 10.
limits: Student samples, small booklets (10 to 11 per booklet in Experiment 2). The authors say Experiment 4 was underpowered for quantifier effects.
agent_relevance: Supports a design rule: do not accept a fit-based plausibility score as a probability. Mismatches between 'more specific, more believable' and 'more specific, less probable' show up in the agent's own claim ranking.

source: Lewinski (2015) Commentary on Tversky & Kahneman 1983. Frontiers in Psychology 6:1832
finding: A 2-page critical comment giving alternative accounts of Linda: people may prefer the richer description of a person, the word 'active' may add meaning, and the choice may be a fast adaptive strategy. Notes the paper was cited about 1,100 times in Web of Science by November 2015.
numbers: 'More than 80 percent of participants failed to recognize the conjunction rule' (as stated in this commentary). Proposes untested experiments (e.g. varying the word 'active').
limits: A commentary with no new data. Cites Hertwig and Gigerenzer 1999 for the claim that the 'error' comes from inferring extra meaning.
agent_relevance: Shows the live dispute: the normative rule is clear but the reading of the wording is not. A model prompt should state the exact question (set inclusion) rather than 'more probable'.

source: Simmons, LeBoeuf & Nelson (2010) The effect of accuracy motivation on anchoring and adjustment. JPSP 99:917-932
finding: Why incentives sometimes fail against anchors: people who are unsure in which direction to adjust believe they have already adjusted too far, so they do not move further. When direction is certain, accuracy motivation does reduce the anchor pull, for provided and self-generated anchors alike.
numbers: Study 1b: for the Miami August temperature question, only 41 percent believed they had adjusted too little when the anchor was plausible (direction unknown); more than half believed it when the anchor was implausible (direction known). Studies 2, 3a, 3b and 5 show the motivation effect appears when direction is known. Study 1a had fewer than half of direction-known subjects believing the adjustment was insufficient, which the authors note does not fully match their prediction.
limits: Ten- and eight-item general-knowledge sets; students. Does not show that anchoring disappears, only that the null for incentives has a boundary condition.
agent_relevance: A warning for the S1 remedy: if an anchor is plausible, telling the model to 'think carefully' will not undo it. The remedy has to be removal by code.

source: Klein et al. (2014) Many Labs 1 - anchoring, as reported from the raw OSF data in an LLM-community write-up
finding: Anchoring replicated in a multi-site test (about 5000 people, four estimation items). In the replication, participants were told the anchor's direction instead of being asked. The effect is real and the group means differ widely.
numbers: Group means, low anchor vs high anchor: babies born per day in the US 3.2k vs 26.7k; Chicago population 1.03m vs 3.00m; Mount Everest height 11.8k vs 34.5k ft; San Francisco to New York 2.85k vs 3.99k miles. The original effect size was a mean point-biserial correlation over 15 questions in a test-retest design; the replication used random assignment, so the effect sizes are not directly comparable.
limits: Secondary source: the blog author rebuilt the table from OSF files. The Many Labs paper itself (Social Psychology 45:142-152) was not opened because the host blocked access. Check the paper before using any d value.
agent_relevance: Anchoring is among the few findings in the Many Labs set that did not shrink. Good reason to keep the S1 anchor-removal step on the schedule.

source: Kahneman & Frederick (2002) Representativeness revisited: attribute substitution in intuitive judgment, in Gilovich, Griffin & Kahneman (eds) Heuristics and Biases, pp 49-81
finding: The unifying theory: a hard target question is answered by a related, easier, more accessible attribute (substitution). Heuristics are cases of attribute substitution. Per the search summary, substitution happens when the target attribute is inaccessible and a related attribute is highly accessible.
numbers: No numbers read. Chapter spans pp 49-81.
limits: Not opened: only a catalogue page and a summary were reached. Do not cite specifics until the chapter text is read.
agent_relevance: The most useful lens for the agent. Substitution means the model answers 'how typical' instead of 'how likely'. S1 can ask 'what is the exact quantity asked' and code can check the answer's units.

source: Gigerenzer (1991) How to make cognitive illusions disappear: beyond heuristics and biases; with Kahneman & Tversky (1996) and Gigerenzer (1996) replies, Psych Review 103:582-596
finding: Main critique of the program. Gigerenzer: many 'errors' come from narrow norms and vague heuristics; single-event vs frequency wording makes them disappear, reappear or invert. Kahneman and Tversky reply that frequency judgments are also biased and that Gigerenzer misreports their position.
numbers: From the search summary: Linda error about 85 percent in probability wording vs about 20 percent in a frequency reformulation (Wikipedia summary of Gigerenzer 1991). The full texts were blocked (HTTP 403), so no numbers were confirmed.
limits: Not opened. The 85 and 20 percent figures come from a secondary summary and should be verified in Fiedler 1988 and Hertwig and Gigerenzer 1999 before use.
agent_relevance: Gives the two sides of the design question: use counts (Gigerenzer) and also assume errors survive in frequency form (K&T). Our agent should test both rather than trust one.

source: Epley & Gilovich (2006) The anchoring-and-adjustment heuristic: why the adjustments are insufficient. Psychological Science 17:311-318
finding: For self-generated anchors, adjustment stops once a plausible value is reached, so it is insufficient unless the person is able and motivated to keep searching. Motivation helps for self-generated anchors, not as clearly for provided ones.
numbers: No numbers read; only the abstract page was reached.
limits: Not opened. Simmons et al. 2010 (a18) re-analyse the provided-vs-self-generated split.
agent_relevance: Gives a mechanism that could map to an LLM: stopping at the first plausible value is the same as taking the first natural answer (S4 no-check path).

source: Zhu & Griffiths (2024) Incoherent probability judgments in large language models. arXiv 2401.16646
finding: Four LLMs (GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, LLaMA-2 7b and 70b) give probability judgments that break probabilistic identities (negation, conjunction, disjunction), as humans do. Repeated judgments show an inverted-U mean-variance relation, like humans. Explained with the Bayesian Sampler model: a few samples plus a prior.
numbers: Four models, events set in 2025. For coherent judgments every identity should equal zero; all four models deviate in the same directions as humans. The model section links autoregressive LLMs to implicit Bayesian inference.
limits: Tested on future events, where no ground truth exists; incoherence is measured, not accuracy. Depends on temperature settings (variants with lower temperature differ).
agent_relevance: A formal model for the whole subfield: judgments are noisy samples pulled to the middle. For the agent, averaging several isolated attempts (S3) moves toward coherence, and code can test the identities directly.

source: Suri, Slater, Ziaee & Nguyen (2023) Do large language models show decision heuristics similar to humans? A case study using GPT-3.5. arXiv 2305.04400
finding: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) showed anchoring, the conjunction fallacy, an availability-style anecdote effect, framing and endowment, and human participants showed similar effects in each of four studies.
numbers: Anchoring (book count estimate, 60 human mTurk participants analysed): ChatGPT means 20.83 (low anchor) vs 105.97 (high anchor), t(58) = 8.78, p < .0001; humans 22.5 vs 80.50, t(58) = 5.55. In 5 trials per condition, GPT-4 gave 22.0 vs 94.33. Conjunction (artist who likes to read): ChatGPT chose the conjunction 18 of 20 times; humans 10 of 20. Framing: human means 5.2 vs 4.6, t(80) = 3.86.
limits: Small trial counts (20 per prompt for the model) and a custom prompt rather than the original Linda text, because ChatGPT knew Linda. Study design confounds memory of the classic with reasoning.
agent_relevance: A first measurement that LLMs get pulled by anchors even harder than humans (105.97 vs 80.50). Supports S1 anchor removal.

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3. PNAS 120(6); arXiv 2206.14576
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci) took the Linda problem, the cab problem, the hospital problem and the CRT. It repeated the human conjunction error and the hospital error, did NOT repeat the cab base-rate error, and gave the intuitive wrong answer on all three CRT items.
numbers: Linda: chose 'bank teller and active feminist' (conjunction fallacy). Cab: gave an approximately correct Bayes answer (people do not). Hospital: 'about equal' (same as people). CRT 1 to 3: intuitive wrong answer on all three. Congruence-bias test: same error as humans. Wason card task: suggested turning A and 7, the correct answer, unlike most people (A and 4).
limits: One model, vignettes likely seen in training. The authors say small perturbations of the vignettes 'can lead GPT-3 vastly astray'.
agent_relevance: A mixed pattern: not all human biases transfer. The agent cannot assume the human list is the model's list; it needs per-class measurement (G7).

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2022/2023) Thinking fast and slow in large language models (CRT and semantic illusions). arXiv 2212.05206
finding: Early GPT-3 models act like System 1 and give the intuitive wrong answer often; ChatGPT-3.5 and GPT-4 avoid it. Chain-of-thought sharply cuts intuitive answers for the earlier model.
numbers: CRT intuitive-wrong share: 80 percent for GPT-3-davinci-003, 55 percent for humans, 15 percent for ChatGPT-3.5, 0 percent for ChatGPT-4. Correct CRT: davinci-003 5 percent, humans 38 percent, ChatGPT-3.5 59 percent, ChatGPT-4 96 percent. Chain-of-thought for davinci-003: correct 5 to 28 percent, intuitive 80 to 29 percent. Blocking chain-of-thought in ChatGPT-4 lowered correct from 95 to 88 percent. Task difficulty checks: model CRT 38 percent correct vs 41 percent in the original human study (n = 3,428).
limits: CRT is not in the heuristics-and-biases list proper, but it is the standard intuition-override test. The prompt versions may have leaked into training.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for G11: for newer models extra reasoning adds little on CRT-style items, and a plain answer already wins.

source: Jones & Steinhardt (2022) Capturing failures of large language models via human cognitive biases. NeurIPS; arXiv 2202.12299
finding: Code models (Codex, CodeGen) show an anchoring-like effect: an erroneous function placed earlier in the prompt lowers accuracy, and parts of it are copied into the output. They also show framing and frequency-of-training-example effects.
numbers: With a print-var anchor function prepended, accuracy fell at every number of canonical lines tested. Codex generated 'for var in' in 32 to 61 percent of solutions and 'print(var)' in 26 to 44 percent when at least one canonical line was shown; the anchor's loop appeared in 3 to 11 percent of correct solutions.
limits: Code generation only; HumanEval prompts; the effect size depends on how many solution lines are given.
agent_relevance: Shows that anchors in S3 context do transfer to open attempts: an earlier attempt shown to a later one contaminates it. Supports the rule that every attempt starts in a fresh context.

source: Lou & Sun (2024) Anchoring bias in large language models: an experimental study. arXiv 2412.06593
finding: GPT-4, GPT-4o and GPT-3.5 Turbo answers shift with biased hints, stronger models included. Chain-of-thought, thoughts of principles, ignoring anchor hints and reflection did not sufficiently mitigate. Collecting hints from comprehensive angles worked better.
numbers: Temperature 0.8; tested on a 60-plus-question dataset with a control and hint conditions (Observation 1: 'stronger models are consistently biased by anchor hints'). In the control runs, GPT-4 and GPT-4o often had zero variance, while about a quarter of GPT-3.5 questions had zero variance.
limits: Two high-school authors; the t-test tables and the exact accuracy values were not cleanly extractable from the PDF text. Treat as qualitative.
agent_relevance: Consistent with section 4b: asking the model to ignore a hint does not remove it. The tested fix that worked (more than one angle) is a code-side pooling of independent inputs.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley & He (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs (BiasBuster). arXiv 2403.00811
finding: A framework with 13,465 prompts across bias types including anchoring, framing, status quo and primacy, tested on admissions-style decisions. Bias-awareness, contrastive and counterfactual prompts were compared with a self-help method where the model rewrites its own prompt.
numbers: Models: Llama-2 7B and 13B, GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4. For anchoring self-help, Llama models changed 40 to 52 percent of their decisions between the sequential and the all-at-once setup. Self-help removed biased elements fully for group attribution bias in GPT-4 and 0 percent remained for framing in Llama-2 13B. Counterfactual and contrastive prompts sometimes produced complete failure cases.
limits: Admissions task is synthetic. Sequential anchoring needs a model that can hold an earlier decision; results depend on capacity.
agent_relevance: A test of 'LLM debiases its own prompt': works only for high-capacity models. Code-side removal does not have this capacity dependence.

source: Macmillan-Scott & Musolesi (2024) (Ir)rationality and cognitive biases in large language models. arXiv 2402.09193
finding: Seven LLMs on classic reasoning tasks including Linda: they are often wrong, but usually NOT in the human biased way, and they give different answers to the same prompt.
numbers: GPT-4 gave the correct answer with correct reasoning in 69.2 percent of cases, Claude 2 in 55.0 percent. Llama-2-7b was wrong in 77.5 percent. GPT-3.5 showed a human-like bias in only 21.7 percent of cases (50.8 percent counting human-like correct answers). GPT-4 gave human-like responses (right or wrong) in 73.3 percent; Llama-2-13b in 8.3 percent.
limits: Small task set per model; the task list was classic material and may be in training data.
agent_relevance: Large inconsistency across runs supports voting and isolated attempts (G4, S3) for any single-answer judgment.

source: Sumita, Takeuchi & Kashima (2024) Cognitive biases in large language models: a survey and mitigation experiments. arXiv 2412.00323
finding: A survey that tabulates which cognitive biases (anchoring, attribute substitution, authority and others) are studied in LLMs and whether mitigation is also tested. Includes mitigation experiments.
numbers: Table 1 maps about 30 related works against bias types and mitigation. The paper was presented as an extended abstract at ACM SAC 2025.
limits: Only the abstract region and table header were read this session; I did not extract its mitigation numbers.
agent_relevance: Use as the index for later reading; it shows that for most biases no mitigation has been tested.

source: Itzhak, Stanovsky, Rosenfeld & Belinkov (2024) Instructed to bias: instruction-tuned language models exhibit emergent cognitive bias. TACL; arXiv 2308.00225
finding: Instruction tuning and RLHF increase cognitive-like biases (decoy effect, certainty effect, belief bias). Instruction-tuned models (Flan-T5, Mistral-Instruct, GPT-3.5, GPT-4) show a stronger presence than their base versions.
numbers: Compared GPT-3, Mistral and T5 families before and after tuning; magnitudes not extracted this session.
limits: Biases tested are decision biases, not the three heuristics proper. Direction (tuning raises bias) is the finding.
agent_relevance: Post-training may add bias; base-model attempts could be a less biased voter, which our equal-token tests can check.

source: Owusu, Wiegreffe & Feldman (2026) Localizing anchoring pathways in language models. arXiv 2606.12818
finding: Irrelevant numbers in a prompt shift LLM multiple-choice answers; circuit analysis on 7B to 8B Qwen and Llama models finds edge-level pathways that carry the anchor signal. Low- and high-anchor circuits transfer within a model, but transfer between base and instruction-tuned variants is unreliable.
numbers: Token-matched 'XXXX' control against low (15) and high (49) anchors on the OpAQ question set. Metric: logit difference between the correct option and the anchor-matching option, validated against behavioural anchoring.
limits: 7B to 8B models only; multiple-choice format with shared options.
agent_relevance: Gives a mechanism: the anchor works as an attribute the model reads off, not as a conscious guess. Token-matched control is a good design for our own S1 test.

source: Kraishan (2026) The long road to the same answer: cognitive bias under escalating reasoning budgets in LLMs. arXiv 2610.10049
finding: Longer thinking does not reduce bias. Across four model families with matched reasoning and non-reasoning siblings at 0, 1,024, 4,096 and 8,192 thinking tokens, reasoning models were not less biased, and bias did not fall as realised thinking grew. Anchoring was the one bias in the human direction.
numbers: 30 vignettes, six biases, 12,350 API calls. Reasoning vs sibling contrast: delta = +0.031, t(29) = 1.45, p = .157. Anchoring d = 1.89. Four of five other biases leaned opposite to the human direction in all seven models. A one-line instruction to restate the anchor before answering lowered anchoring on all five items (p = .057).
limits: Only five items per bias; the restate-the-anchor effect is not significant. Vignettes from an existing benchmark, possibly in training data.
agent_relevance: Strongest recent support for G11 and for S1: more thinking does not undo an anchor, and a cheap restatement step might. Test restate-the-anchor at equal tokens.

source: Huang et al. (2026) CogBias: measuring and mitigating cognitive bias in large language models. arXiv 2604.01366
finding: Benchmark of four bias families (Judgment, Information Processing, Social, Response) on GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.3-70B and Qwen2.5-72B. Prompt debiasing helps Response biases but backfires for Judgment biases (base rate, anchoring, sunk cost, status quo). Linear probes find bias directions; steering cut bias score 26 to 32 percent.
numbers: Baseline Judgment bias shifts: GPT -4.3, Llama -7.7, Qwen -2.7 percentage points. Debiasing effect: Judgment about -4.4 percent (backfire) vs Response +40.5 percent. Response family: 78.1 percent first-option rate vs 36.8 percent chance. Steering cost on Qwen: up to -19.0 points of capability for Judgment biases; Llama negligible.
limits: Three models, one prompt-level debiasing recipe; the setup is paired with and without a trigger. Steering is not available for closed models.
agent_relevance: Judgment biases, the ones in this subfield, are the hardest to fix by prompt. Backs the section 4b ban on debiasing instructions and the choice of code-side hygiene.

source: Wang et al. (2026) Making bias non-predictive: training robust LLM reasoning via reinforcement learning (EIT). arXiv 2602.01528
finding: Reasoning models reverse correct answers when given a fabricated consensus or authority cue. Prompting and supervised fine-tuning fail to generalise. Reinforcement learning that makes bias cues equally likely to support right and wrong answers improves robustness, and transfers from bandwagon to authority and distraction cues.
numbers: Trained on Qwen3-4B; also tested on Llama-3.2-3B and Qwen3-8B, and on MedQA and HellaSwag.
limits: Training-based, so outside our no-training constraint. Numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Confirms that the cues are non-causal yet change the answer; for us the equivalent is code removal in S1.

source: Do chains-of-thought of LLMs suffer from hallucinations, cognitive biases, or phobias in Bayesian reasoning? arXiv 2503.15268
finding: Reasoning LLMs do not spontaneously use natural frequencies, whole objects or embodied heuristics in Bayesian problems, unlike people. When prompted to, they use them, but not consistently, and show a persistent bias toward symbolic reasoning.
numbers: No numbers extracted in this pass; qualitative abstract result across several LLMs with chain-of-thought.
limits: Teaching-oriented paper. Small number of problems.
agent_relevance: Bears on the frequency-format idea (a13): the model will not choose counts by itself, so code has to supply the count form.
